        AMERICAN STEWARDS OF LIBERTY’S RESPONSE TO BRIEFING ON
           REMANDED PRELIMINARY ORDER ISSUE NOS. 11 AND 13

        COMES NOW, American Stewards of Liberty (ASL) and files its Response to Briefing on

 Remanded Preliminary Order (PO) Issue Nos. 11 and 13, and in support thereof, shows as follows.

                                     I.   INTRODUCTION

        Commission Staff’s and Oncor Electric Delivery Company LLC and LCRA Transmission

 Service Corporation’s (collectively, the Applicants) respective briefs on remand suffer from the
 same fundamental deficiency: neither identifies evidence establishing that Import Path 2 is

necessary to meet state or federal reliability standards or quantifies the congestion-cost savings

attributable to the proposed facilities. Instead, both rely on ERCOT’s system-wide planning

studies and the Commission’s prior approval of the Permian Basin Reliability Plan (PBRP) to

establish the necessity of Import Path 2. Their arguments rest on the same flawed premise—that

because the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) identified reliability concerns in the

Permian Basin and recommended a comprehensive state-wide 765-kV transmission solution,

every component of that solution must necessarily be needed. But that is precisely the assumption

that the Proposal for Decision (PFD) correctly rejected.

        The Commission remanded this proceeding for further consideration of Preliminary Order

(PO) Issue Nos. 11 and 13. The evidentiary record was and remains closed. Accordingly, the task

before the SOAH ALJs is limited to: (a) determining whether the existing record establishes that

Import Path 2 is necessary to meet state or federal reliability standards; and (b) identifying the

estimated congestion-cost savings to consumers resulting from the proposed facilities. The remand

does not relieve Applicants of their burden to establish project-specific need under PURA

§ 37.056, nor does it authorize the substitution of ERCOT’s planning recommendations for the

evidence necessary to satisfy that burden.

        Yet that is precisely what Staff and Applicants ask the SOAH ALJs to do. Both devote

considerable attention to the reliability violations identified by ERCOT, the development of the

PBRP, and subsequent ERCOT studies incorporating the 765-kV buildout. Neither, however,

establishes that Import Path 2 is independently necessary to remedy an identified reliability

violation. Indeed, Applicants expressly acknowledge that the record contains no technical analysis

modeling a reliable alternative with Import Path 2 removed. Rather than recognize that omission




ASL Response to Briefing on Remanded Preliminary Order Issues                               Page 2
 as an evidentiary deficiency, Applicants attempt to turn it into affirmative proof of necessity. Their

position effectively shifts the burden to opponents of the Project to demonstrate that Import Path

2 is unnecessary, rather than requiring Applicants to establish that it is.

        Equally significant is what neither brief meaningfully addresses. The PFD found that

Applicants failed to establish whether sufficient generation would be available at Bell County East

to simultaneously serve projected Central Texas load growth and supply the westward imports

contemplated by Import Path 2. That finding goes directly to whether the proposed facilities can

perform their asserted reliability function per PO Issue No. 11. Yet Staff and Applicants offer no

analysis resolving that deficiency. Applicants instead emphasize that Import Path 2 will operate

bidirectionally, while Staff relies on successive ERCOT planning studies. Neither argument

establishes that sufficient generation will be available to support the asserted import function when

it is needed.

        Applicants’ and Staff’s remand briefing on PO Issue No. 13 are similarly deficient. Staff

relies on economic comparisons between the comprehensive 345-kV and 765-kV transmission

plans, while Applicants emphasize projected consumer benefits associated with the entire 765-kV

buildout. But neither identifies an estimate of congestion-cost savings attributable to Import Path

2. Their reliance on portfolio-wide economic benefits does not answer the Commission’s project-

specific question, and their assertion that congestion-cost savings are unnecessary for reliability

projects presupposes the very reliability determination that the PFD found unsupported.

        Perhaps most revealing is Applicants’ reliance on the Commission’s recent approval of

Import Paths 1 and 3. Applicants contend that because those projects were approved based on the

same PBRP and ERCOT studies, there is no valid reason to reach a different conclusion concerning

Import Path 2.      They further acknowledge, in their proposed findings, that they did not




ASL Response to Briefing on Remanded Preliminary Order Issues                                   Page 3
 independently evaluate alternatives because the Commission had already approved the PBRP and

directed the filing of CCN applications. These arguments expose the fundamental problem with

the approach advocated by both Staff and Applicants: they treat the Commission’s approval of a

regional reliability plan as having already resolved the project-specific determination of need that

is statutorily required in these proceedings.

           The Commission’s prior approval of other transmission projects cannot supply evidence

missing from this record. Nor can the repetition of ERCOT’s planning conclusions across

successive studies transform an untested assumption into proof of necessity. PURA § 37.056

requires more than a showing that a proposed project was included in a preferred regional

transmission plan. It requires a determination, supported by the evidence, that the particular

facilities proposed are necessary.

           The PFD correctly concluded that Applicants failed to make that showing. Neither Staff’s

nor Applicants’ briefing provides a basis to disturb that determination.

                               II.     RESPONSE TO COMMISSION STAFF

A.         Staff’s Reliance on ERCOT’s Reliability Studies Does Not Establish That Import
           Path 2 is Necessary to Meet State or Federal Reliability Standards

           Staff answers PO Issue No. 11 affirmatively, asserting that the proposed facilities are

necessary to meet state and federal reliability standards because ERCOT identified widespread

thermal and voltage violations, voltage instability, and unsolved power-flow conditions under

NERC Reliability Standard TPL-001-5.1 and ERCOT planning criteria. 1 Staff further contends

that ERCOT’s subsequent reliability assessments consistently demonstrate the necessity of the

765-kV buildout, including Import Path 2. 2



1
    Commission Staff’s Initial Brief on Remand at 2 (Oct. 7, 2026) (Staff Brief).
2
    Id. at 3.


ASL Response to Briefing on Remanded Preliminary Order Issues                                 Page 4
            But Staff’s argument conflates two distinct propositions: that ERCOT identified reliability

violations requiring corrective action and that Import Path 2 is itself necessary to remedy those

violations. The first proposition does not establish the second.

           There is no dispute that ERCOT performed reliability assessments under NERC and

ERCOT planning criteria or that those assessments identified transmission-system constraints.

The question presented by PO Issue No. 11, however, is whether “the proposed transmission

facilities” are necessary to meet state or federal reliability standards. 3 That question requires more

than identifying the planning standards ERCOT applied or the reliability concerns that prompted

development of the PBRP. It requires evidence establishing the necessity of the particular facilities

proposed in these applications.

           Staff identifies no specific violation of TPL-00l-5.1 that can be remedied only through

Import Path 2. Nor does Staff identify an analysis establishing that the Bell County East-to-Big

Hill and Big Hill-to-Sand Lake facilities are independently necessary to maintain compliance with

an identified reliability standard. Instead, Staff relies on ERCOT’s conclusion that the 765-kV

buildout, considered as a whole, is needed to increase import capability into the Permian Basin.

           Staff’s reasoning assumes the very conclusion Applicants were required to establish. The

fact that Import Path 2 was included in ERCOT’s preferred transmission solution does not establish

that Import Path 2 is independently necessary, particularly when the record does not demonstrate

that ERCOT evaluated whether the identified reliability concerns could be resolved without those

facilities.

           Applicants’ own witness acknowledged that the individual lines were not studied

independently. When asked whether ERCOT had isolated each line in its analysis, Mr. Gurley



3
    PO at Issue No. 11 (Mar. 30, 2026) (emphasis added).


ASL Response to Briefing on Remanded Preliminary Order Issues                                    Page 5
 testified: “I am not aware of a study that isolated each line independently as they were—they were

studied together.” 4 That admission is directly consistent with the PFD’s findings that Applicants

“did not perform a partial build study to justify the need for Import Path 2 individually” and “did

not establish the need for Import Path 2 separate and apart from the three 765-kV import paths as

one comprehensive project.” 5

        Staff’s remand briefing fails to address that testimony or those findings. It does not identify

a partial-build analysis, a with-and-without-Import Path 2 reliability assessment, or any other

evidence establishing that the particular facilities proposed in these applications are required to

satisfy an identified reliability standard. Rather, Staff simply repeats the broader ERCOT planning

conclusions that the SOAH ALJs already considered and rejected.

        Staff’s reliance on the 2024 and 2025 Regional Transmission Plans (RTPs) suffers from

the same defect. Staff contends that successive ERCOT studies consistently demonstrate the need

for the 765-kV buildout. 6 But consistency among planning studies does not establish independent

verification of a particular project’s necessity when those studies incorporate the same underlying

assumptions.

        Critically, the 2025 RTP incorporated the entire 765-kV Strategic Transmission Expansion

Plan (STEP) into its starting base cases. 7 A study that assumes the proposed infrastructure as part

of the starting transmission topology cannot independently establish that every component of that

infrastructure is necessary. It assumes the very facilities whose necessity must be determined.

        Staff’s reliance on ERCOT’s Generic Transmission Constraint (GTC) exit strategies is

similarly unpersuasive. The existence of the North-to-Far-West and South-to-Far-West Import


4
  June 8, 2026 Hearing on the Merits Tr. at 44:21-45:4.
5
  PFD at 180, FOF Nos. 128-130.
6
  Staff Brief at 3.
7
  Applicants’ Ex. 17 (Gurley Rebuttal), Ex. JG-R-3 (2025 RTP) at 28.


ASL Response to Briefing on Remanded Preliminary Order Issues                                    Page 6
 GTCs establishes that operational constraints exist in Far West Texas. It does not establish that

Import Path 2 is independently required to resolve those constraints. ERCOT’s exit strategies

identify multiple projects, including six projects for the North-to-Far-West GTC and eight for the

South-to-Far-West GTC. 8 Staff does not explain whether those constraints could be resolved

without Import Path 2 or identify evidence establishing that Import Path 2 is indispensable to their

resolution.

           The PFD expressly considered the GTC evidence and determined that it did not establish

the necessity of Import Path 2. Among other things, the SOAH ALJs found that the GTC evidence

did not validate the composition or reliability of the load underlying the PBRP forecast and did

not establish the necessity of Import Path 2. 9 Staff’s briefing supplies no reason to disturb those

evidence-based findings.

           Ultimately, Staff’s position reduces PO Issue No. 11 to the proposition that because

ERCOT conducted reliability studies and recommended Import Path 2 as part of a broader

transmission solution, Import Path 2 must be necessary to meet reliability standards. That is not a

project-specific determination of necessity. It is deference to ERCOT’s planning recommendation

in place of the evidentiary showing required by PURA § 37.056.

B.         Staff Does Not Address the PFD’s Findings that Applicants Failed to Establish
           Whether Import Path 2 Can Perform Its Asserted Reliability Function

           Staff’s briefing also fails to confront the Applicants’ most fundamental evidentiary

deficiency supporting the PFD’s determination that Applicants failed to establish need: the absence

of evidence demonstrating that sufficient generation will be available at Bell County East to

perform the westward-import function on which the asserted necessity of Import Path 2 depends.



8
    Applicants’ Ex. 14 (Martin Rebuttal) at 16-17.
9
    PFD at 178-79, FOF Nos. 112-16.


ASL Response to Briefing on Remanded Preliminary Order Issues                                 Page 7
            Staff argues that the 765-kV buildout is needed to increase import capability into the

Permian Basin and support reliable service. 10 But increased transmission capacity standing alone

has zero effect on reliability. Transmission facilities can move electricity only if generation is

available to produce power. If the asserted reliability function of Import Path 2 is to transfer power

from Central Texas into the Permian Basin during periods of insufficient local generation, then the

reliability of that solution necessarily depends upon the availability of generation at the eastern

end of the proposed facilities.

           The SOAH ALJs expressly identified this deficiency. The PFD found that Applicants

failed to establish that sufficient power would be available at Bell County East to transmit

westward over Import Path 2. Neither Applicants nor ERCOT analyzed Central Texas’s net

generation position under current conditions, projected 2030 conditions, or projected conditions

incorporating substantial queued large loads. Nor did Applicants determine whether Central Texas

generation could simultaneously serve local data-center demand and export power westward. Nor

did Applicants or ERCOT perform a sensitivity analysis evaluating the viability of Import Path 2

if generation in Central Texas proved to be insufficient to perform both functions. 11

           These PFD findings go directly to the reliability function Staff attributes to the Project.

Yet Staff’s remand briefing simply fails to address them.

           The significance of these omissions is underscored by the ongoing uncertainty surrounding

large-load development in Central Texas. On October 14, 2026, Rowan Stampede, LLC filed a

complaint against ERCOT in PUC Docket No. 60396 challenging ERCOT’s reclassification of its

Project Stampede data-center development in Temple, Bell County, from Base Load to Studied




10
     Staff Brief at 2-3.
11
     PFD at 179-80, FOF Nos. 121-26.


ASL Response to Briefing on Remanded Preliminary Order Issues                                   Page 8
 Load under the Batch Zero process. 12 Rowan alleges that ERCOT reclassified the project

notwithstanding its prior approval of the project’s interconnection studies, based on additional

large loads that ERCOT subsequently determined should have been included in the study

assumptions. Notably, Rowan identifies Project Stampede as a large-load development included

in ERCOT’s 2025 RTP. 13

          While ASL does not rely upon the allegations in Rowan’s complaint as evidence, the

complaint illustrates the continuing disputes surrounding the treatment of substantial large loads

in Central Texas, including loads previously incorporated into ERCOT’s planning process. The

relevance to the present proceeding is the unresolved question already identified in the PFD:

whether sufficient generation will be available at Bell County East to simultaneously serve

substantial Central Texas load growth and supply the westward imports contemplated by Import

Path 2.

          Staff’s reliance on successive ERCOT planning studies does not resolve that question. The

repetition of planning conclusions does not establish the reliability of the assumptions underlying

those conclusions, particularly where Applicants failed to evaluate how changes in generation

availability or competing local loads would affect the asserted need for Import Path 2.

          Nor can Staff overcome the PFD’s findings by simply labeling Import Path 2 as a reliability

project. The reliability classification depends upon the existence of a reliable solution to an

identified problem. If Applicants have not established that sufficient generation will be available

to perform the asserted import function, Staff cannot establish the necessity of that function merely

by identifying the reliability standards governing ERCOT’s planning studies.


12
   Complaint, Request for Immediate Suspension of Conduct, and Request for Expedited Relief of Rowan Stampede
LLC Against the Electric Reliability Council of Texas, Inc., PUC Docket No. 60396, at 2-4 (Oct. 14, 2026) (Rowan
Complaint).
13
   Id. at 15-18 and Ex. D.


ASL Response to Briefing on Remanded Preliminary Order Issues                                              Page 9
            The SOAH ALJs therefore correctly found that “the record does not establish that Import

Path 2 is needed for reliability.” 14 Staff’s briefing does not identify any evidence contradicting

that determination.

C.         Staff’s Economic Evidence Does Not Quantify Congestion-Cost Savings Attributable
           to Import Path 2

           Staff’s remand briefing on PO Issue No. 13 is equally deficient. Staff first contends that

because Import Path 2 qualifies as a reliability project under 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(A)(ii), an

evaluation       of   congestion-cost   savings     under       the   economic-project   provisions   of

§ 25.101(b)(3)(A)(i) is unnecessary. 15 Alternatively, Staff argues that the record demonstrates

congestion-cost savings may result from Import Path 2 because ERCOT’s comparison of the

345-kV and 765-kV transmission plans shows favorable long-term economic results for the

765-kV plan. Neither argument answers the question presented by PO Issue No. 13.

           Staff’s primary argument depends upon the premise that Import Path 2 qualifies as a

reliability project. But that premise is precisely what the PFD rejected. Applicants failed to

establish the need for Import Path 2, and Staff’s reliance on ERCOT’s system-wide reliability

studies does not cure that deficiency. Staff therefore cannot simply label the project “reliability”

and then rely on that characterization as the basis for foreclosing consideration of whether the

record provides an alternative economic justification for approval.

           ASL does not contend that every reliability project must independently satisfy the

economic-project criteria. Rather, the issue on remand is whether the existing record establishes

the estimated congestion-cost savings to consumers resulting from the proposed facilities. If, as

implicated by the Commission’s remand, the economic evidence could provide an alternative basis



14
     PFD at 180, FOF No. 127.
15
     Staff Brief at 3.


ASL Response to Briefing on Remanded Preliminary Order Issues                                    Page 10
 for finding need, then that evidence must actually establish the relevant benefit. The possibility

that Import Path 2 may produce some economic benefit is not a substitute for an estimate

attributable to the Project.

            Staff’s alternative argument fails for that reason. Staff relies on ERCOT’s comparison of

the entire 765-kV STEP with an alternative 345-kV transmission plan. That comparison evaluates

two comprehensive transmission portfolios. It does not compare the ERCOT system with and

without Import Path 2, isolate the Bell County East-to-Big Hill and Big Hill-to-Sand Lake

facilities, or determine the incremental congestion-cost savings attributable to those facilities.

            Staff acknowledges that the 345-kV plan produces greater consumer-energy-cost savings

than the 765-kV plan in 2034. Specifically, Staff cites estimate consumer-energy costs of

$18.143 billion under the 345-kV plan and $18.279 billion under the 765-kV plan, compared to

$18.342 billion under ERCOT’s baseline scenario. Thus, while both transmission alternatives

produce modeled savings relative to the baseline, the 345-kV plan produces approximately

$199 million in savings, compared to only $63 million under the 765-kV plan. 16 Put differently,

the 345-kV alternative produces approximately $136 million more in consumer-energy cost

savings than the 765-kV alternative.

            Staff emphasizes that the 765-kV plan performs better in 2039, when ERCOT estimates

consumer-energy costs of $21.914 billion under the 765-kV plan compared to $22.143 billion

under the 345-kV plan. 17 But even accepting these projections, the comparison remains based on

entire transmission portfolios. It does not establish what portion of the projected benefit, if any, is

attributable to Import Path 2.




16
     Id. at 4.
17
     Id. at 4 n. 10.


ASL Response to Briefing on Remanded Preliminary Order Issues                                  Page 11
         Staff’s reliance on congestion rent further illustrates the problem. Staff asserts that

reductions in congestion rent under the 765-kV plan demonstrate that the proposed facilities will

reduce congestion costs for consumers. 18 But the ERCOT study distinguishes between production

costs, consumer-energy costs, and congestion rent. Those measures are not interchangeable.

        Staff does not explain how the congestion-rent reduction it identifies translate into the

particular consumer congestion-cost savings requested by PO Issue No. 13. More importantly,

Staff does not establish how any portion of those portfolio-wide reductions can be attributed to

Import Path 2.

        The distinction is critical. PO Issue No. 13 does not ask whether congestion exists in

ERCOT, whether additional transmission capacity could alleviate congestion, or whether the entire

765-kV STEP may produce greater long-term economic benefits than an alternative transmission

portfolio. It asks for the estimated congestion-cost savings for consumers that may result from the

proposed transmission facilities. 19 Staff supplies no such estimate.

        Indeed, Staff’s briefing states only that congestion-cost savings “may result from the

projects” and that the 765-kV plan, including Import Path 2, “will help reduce congestion levels

and thereby reduce congestion costs for consumers.” 20 Those statements describe potential

qualitative benefits. They do not quantify the savings attributable to Import Path 2.

        The PFD already recognized this deficiency, finding that Applicants did not submit the

requested estimate of congestion-cost savings to consumers. 21          Staff identifies no analysis

contradicting that finding. Its reliance on portfolio-wide economic predictions does not transform

those results into a project-specific estimate.


18
   Id. at 4.
19
   PO at Issue No. 13.
20
   Staff Brief at 4.
21
   PFD at 149-50, 191, FOF Nos. 226-227.


ASL Response to Briefing on Remanded Preliminary Order Issues                                Page 12
           Accordingly, the supplemental PFD should retain the determination that the record

contains no quantified estimate of congestion-cost savings to consumers attributable to Import

Path 2.

D.        Staff’s Briefing Provides No Basis to Disturb the PFD’s Original Determination of
          Need

          The deficiencies in Staff’s briefing are not matters of form. They concern the substantive

evidence necessary to establish the need for Import Path 2.

          As to PO Issue No. 11, Staff identifies the reliability standards ERCOT considered and the

system-wide planning studies supporting the broader 765-kV buildout. It does not establish that

Import Path 2 is independently necessary to satisfy an identified reliability standard. Staff does

not address Applicants’ failure to provide partial-build analysis, the PFD’s findings concerning the

Far West GTCs, or the absence of evidence establishing generation availability at Bell County

East.

          As to PO Issue No. 13, Staff relies on the economic performance of the entire 765-kV

STEP, but does not identify an estimate of congestion-cost savings attributable to Import Path 2.

Its argument that the Project qualifies as a reliability project cannot supply the missing economic

evidence, particularly where the PFD found that Applicants failed to establish reliability need.

          These are the same evidentiary deficiencies the SOAH ALJs considered in reaching their

original determination. Staff does not identify new record evidence that resolves them. Nor does

Staff demonstrate that the PFD overlooked evidence that would support a different result.

          The Commission’s remand requires the SOAH ALJs to provide more explicit answers to

PO Issue Nos. 11 and 13. It does not authorize the Commission or Staff to transform ERCOT’s

planning assumptions into findings of project-specific necessity or to attribute portfolio-wide

economic benefits to facilities that were never independently evaluated.



ASL Response to Briefing on Remanded Preliminary Order Issues                                Page 13
            The supplemental PFD should therefore clarify, rather than alter, the original findings. The

record does not establish that Import Path 2 is necessary to meet an identified state or federal

reliability standard. It does not contain an estimate of congestion-cost savings to consumers

attributable to Import Path 2. And it does not establish that sufficient generation will be available

at Bell County East to perform the westward-import function upon which Applicants’ asserted

reliability need depends.

           Staff’s briefing provides no basis to conclude otherwise.

                                    III.     RESPONSE TO APPLICANTS

A.         PO Issue No. 11

           1.       Applicants’ Identification of Reliability Violations Does Not Establish That Import
                    Path 2 is Necessary to Remedy Those Violations.

           Applicants devote considerable attention to the federal reliability framework governing

ERCOT’s planning responsibilities. They discuss NERC Reliability Standard TPL-001-5.1,

describe thermal overloads, voltage instability, and unsolvable power-flow contingencies, and

explain the consequences of failing to maintain a reliable bulk-power system. 22

           ASL does not dispute that ERCOT must comply with applicable reliability standards or

that identified reliability violations require appropriate corrective action. The dispute concerns

whether Applicants established that the particular facilities proposed in these applications

constitute that appropriate corrective action.

           Applicants collapse those separate inquiries into one. They contend that because ERCOT’s

studies identified reliability violations and the PBRP included Import Path 2 among the projects

recommended to resolve those violations, Import Path 2 is necessarily a reliability project. 23 But



22
     Applicants’ Brief on Preliminary Order Issue Nos. 11 and 13 at 4-7 (Oct. 7, 2026) (Applicants’ Brief).
23
     Id. at 4, 6-8.


ASL Response to Briefing on Remanded Preliminary Order Issues                                                 Page 14
 inclusion in a recommended solution does not separately establish that every component of that

solution is necessary.

           PURA § 37.056 requires the Commission to determine whether the proposed facilities are

necessary for the service, accommodation, convenience, or safety of the public. The statute does

not permit Applicants to satisfy that requirement merely by demonstrating that ERCOT identified

a regional reliability problem. Nor does 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(A)(ii)(II), which affords great

weight to ERCOT’s recommendation concerning a reliability project, transform that

recommendation into a conclusive determination of need for Import Path 2, a distinct component

of the plan.

           Applicants’ position would effectively eliminate the distinction between ERCOT’s

planning responsibilities and the Commission’s statutory obligation to determine need in a CCN

proceeding. Once ERCOT recommended a transmission project and the Commission approved

the broader planning framework, no further showing of necessity would be required. The CCN

proceeding would become little more than a mechanism for selecting a route. That is not the

process established by PURA § 37.056.

           The record demonstrates why the distinction matters here.                       Applicants’ witness

acknowledged that ERCOT did not independently study each line comprising the import paths. 24

The PFD expressly recognized this deficiency, finding that Applicants did not perform a partial-

build study justifying the need for Import Path 2 individually and did not establish the need for

Import Path 2 separate and apart from the three 765-kV import paths considered as one

comprehensive project. 25




24
     June 8, 2026 Hearing on the Merits Tr. at 44:21-45:4; Applicants’ Brief at 11 n.40.
25
     PFD at 180, FOF Nos. 128-130.


ASL Response to Briefing on Remanded Preliminary Order Issues                                          Page 15
            Applicants’ briefing fails identify any record evidence contradicting those findings.

Rather, Applicants attempt to turn the absence of an independent analysis into an affirmative

justification for approval. They instead argue that the record contains no power-flow study or

other technical analysis demonstrating a reliable alternative with Import Path 2 removed and that

removing Import Path 2 would introduce an untested variable into ERCOT’s planning process. 26

           Yet the absence of an analysis demonstrating that Import Path 2 can be removed without

compromising reliability does nothing to establish that Import Path 2 must be constructed. At its

essence, Applicants’ theory appears to be that their failure to perform the technical analysis proves

that the analysis need not be performed. The burden to establish the necessity of the facilities for

which they seek certification lies solely with Applicants. It was neither ASL’s burden nor the

affected landowners’ burden to develop an alternative transmission model disproving ERCOT’s

preferred solution.

           Applicants’ argument is particularly troubling because, if adopted, it would effectively

immunize ERCOT’s initial selection of a transmission portfolio from scrutiny. By studying the

import paths together and subsequently incorporating them into future planning models, ERCOT

could ensure that no independent analysis existed against which to test the necessity of an

individual project. As Applicants attempt here, future CCN applicants could simply invoke the

absence of line-specific evidence as justification for approving every component of the portfolio.

           The Commissions should not permit the absence of the very analysis needed to establish

project-specific necessity to become the basis for finding that necessity exists.




26
     Applicants’ Brief at 11-12.


ASL Response to Briefing on Remanded Preliminary Order Issues                                 Page 16
         2.       The Subsequent ERCOT Studies Do Not Independently Establish the Need for
                 Import Path 2.

        Applicants contend that four ERCOT planning efforts—the PBRP, the 2024 RTP, the

2025 RTP, and the April 2026 GTC exit strategy---consistently establish the necessity of Import

Path 2. 27 The number of studies, however, does not resolve whether those studies independently

evaluated the necessity of the proposed facilities. They did not.

        Applicants acknowledge that the 2025 RTP incorporated the three 765-kV import paths

into its starting baseline scenario. 28 That is significant. A study that assumes the construction of

Import Path 2 as part of the baseline transmission system cannot, without additional analysis,

independently establish that Import Path 2 is necessary.

        The fact that subsequent planning studies continue to include facilities previously selected

through the PBRP does not transform the original planning recommendation into independent

evidence of project-specific necessity. It demonstrates that ERCOT continued its planning based

on its pre-determined transmission solution.

        Applicants’ reliance on the 2024 RTP does not cure the deficiency. Applicants identify

the RTP’s designation of Import Path 2 as part of the 765-kV Core Plan needed in 2030. 29 But

that designation does not identify a reliability violation that Import Path 2 alone is necessary to

remedy, nor does it establish whether the identified reliability concerns could be addressed through

a different combination of transmission improvements or generation resources.

        Applicants also emphasize ERCOT’s April 2026 GTC exit strategy identifies all three

import paths as necessary to retire the Far West Texas Import GTCs. 30 Yet the exit strategy, like



27
   Id. at 9-12.
28
   Id. at 9-11; Applicants’ Ex. 17 (Gurley Rebuttal), Ex. JG-R-3 at 28-33, 100.
29
   Applicants’ Brief at 9; Applicants’ Ex. 17 (Gurley Rebuttal), Ex. JG-R-2 at 62.
30
   Applicants’ Brief at 8-9; Applicants’ Ex. 14 (Martin Rebuttal), Ex. CMM-R-5 at 41-44.


ASL Response to Briefing on Remanded Preliminary Order Issues                                 Page 17
 the broader planning studies, evaluates a collection of transmission improvements. Applicants do

not identify an analysis isolating the contribution of Import Path 2 or establishing that the GTCs

cannot be resolved without those particular facilities.

           The PFD considered the GTC evidence and nevertheless concluded that Applicants had
